metadata.summary: This EANO guideline updates recommendations for diagnosing, classifying, treating and monitoring meningiomas, including intracranial and spinal tumors across WHO grades. It addresses imaging, histopathology, molecular findings, observation, surgery, radiation approaches and pharmacotherapy, while considering cognition and quality of life. The guideline notes that systemic treatments remain experimental and that no standard systemic therapy has been established.

care_settings: Treatment of recurrent or inoperable tumors
target_population: Patients with suspected or diagnosed meningiomas
Patients with incidental or asymptomatic meningiomas
Patients with symptomatic or growing meningiomas
Patients with recurrent or inoperable meningiomas

prevention: Preoperative embolization is not recommended as routine practice; individual decisions are left to the surgical team.

toxicities.event: Seizures and hydrocephalus as surgical risks
prevention: Discuss these general surgical risks with patients before the operation.
Plan surgery with particular attention to neurovascular anatomy.
Prioritize preservation of neurological function over gross total resection when the latter cannot be achieved safely.
Intra-operative neurophysiological monitoring may help reduce neurological deficits.

recognition: Difficulties involving memory, attention, and executive functions
Patients with substantial preoperative cerebral edema may experience longer-term postoperative cognitive limitations.
prevention: Consider potential short- and long-term cognitive effects when deciding on surgery.
Do not pursue gross total resection at the expense of cognitive function.

toxicities.event: Long-term deterioration in health-related quality of life after surgery
prevention: Consider possible short- and long-term effects on health-related quality of life when deciding on surgery.

toxicities.event: Cranial nerve function deterioration after SRS
toxicities.incidence: In a registry-based analysis of 150 patients treated with resection and SRS for skull base meningiomas, deterioration occurred in 3.5% after 1 year, 5.5% after 3 years, 7% after 5 years, and 10% 10 years after SRS.
The reported risk is considered low, at 6.8 cases per 100 000 patient-years.

prevention: Weigh these potential long-term risks against the possible benefit of avoiding further surgery.

toxicities.event: Adverse events in the intermediate-risk cohort of NRG Oncology/RTOG 0539
toxicities.incidence: The report describes adverse events limited to grade 1 and 2; it does not provide an incidence.

toxicities.event: Acute and late adverse events in the high-risk cohort of NRG Oncology/RTOG 0539
toxicities.incidence: Combined acute and late adverse events occurred in about 40% of patients and were limited to CTCAE grades 1-3, apart from 1 death related to necrosis.
toxicities.grading: CTCAE (Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events)

toxicities.incidence: Late toxicity of grade 3 or more was observed in 14% of patients.

recommendations.statement: Use MRI to establish the radiological diagnosis of meningioma.
Obtain somatostatin receptor II-directed PET when the extent of the tumor or the presence of recurrence is uncertain.
recommendations.rationale: This technique detects meningioma with high sensitivity and specificity.

recommendations.statement: Acquire tumor tissue for molecular analysis.
recommendations.rationale: Molecular findings have prognostic relevance and may enable future targeted treatment.

recommendations.statement: Choose observation initially for asymptomatic patients with a newly diagnosed or slowly growing meningioma.
Assess memory, attention, and executive function, and incorporate the findings into treatment decisions.
Take potential treatment-related impairment of HRQoL into account whenever deciding whether to treat.
When treatment is indicated, consider surgery first for tumors of any WHO grade.
Aim for gross total resection according to Simpson Grade I when it can be accomplished safely.
Consider radiosurgery instead of surgery for small tumors in particular locations or clinical circumstances when obtaining tissue is not essential.
Treat WHO grade 1 meningiomas requiring intervention with radiosurgery or fractionated radiosurgery when surgery is not feasible.
Patients without neurological deficits after incomplete resection of a WHO grade 1 meningioma may be followed with observation and imaging.
Administer fractionated radiotherapy to patients with recurrent or atypical meningiomas.
Consider planned subtotal resection followed by radiosurgery or fractionated radiotherapy for comprehensive treatment of WHO grade 1 meningiomas with a lower risk of progression.
Treat WHO grade 3 meningiomas with radical surgery and fractionated radiotherapy.
Consider bevacizumab or multikinase inhibitors targeting VEGF receptors only when no further local treatment is available.
Perform follow-up MRI for WHO grade 1 meningiomas every 12 months, then every 2 years after 5 years.
Perform follow-up MRI for WHO grade 2 meningiomas every 6 months, then every 12 months after 5 years.
Tailor follow-up of WHO grade 3 meningiomas to clinical progression, with assessments at least every 3-6 months.
Base routine imaging surveillance on gadolinium-enhanced, T1-weighted MRI sequences; follow-up using only T2-weighted imaging may be considered for small meningiomas.
recommendations.rationale: T2-weighted axial MRI provides size measurements comparable to those from gadolinium-enhanced T1 imaging.

recommendations.statement: For incidentally identified, asymptomatic WHO grade 1 meningiomas, initially observe with annual MRI.
Administer RT after Simpson IV-V resection of a WHO grade 2 meningioma.
recommendations.rationale: These tumors carry an increased risk of recurrence.

recommendations.statement: Use surgical resection as the preferred treatment for spinal meningiomas, aiming for Simpson grade I or II resection; attempt gross total resection in elderly patients as well.
recommendations.rationale: Resection removes the tumor and decompresses the spinal cord.

therapies_index.name: observation
approved_indications: Initial management of incidental, asymptomatic suspected meningiomas and newly diagnosed or slowly growing meningiomas without symptoms.
An option after incomplete resection of WHO grade 1 meningiomas, particularly when neurological symptoms or signs do not persist.
An option after gross total resection of WHO grade 1 or WHO grade 2 meningiomas.
therapies_index.administration: Serial MRI is used; for suspected meningiomas or WHO grade 1 meningiomas, annual scans are recommended for 5 years, after which the intervals may be extended.
monitoring: MRI surveillance.
Assessment of neurological status and cognitive impairment.

therapies_index.name: surgery
approved_indications: First treatment option when a meningioma is symptomatic, enlarging, or otherwise requires intervention.
First option for WHO grade 2 meningioma to obtain diagnostic tissue and relieve mass effect.
Treatment of choice for spinal meningioma.
therapies_index.administration: Resection should maximize safe tumor removal while preserving neurological and cognitive function; tissue can be retained for molecular testing.
key_toxicities: Neurological or cognitive impairment may occur after surgery.
Risks discussed with patients include seizures and hydrocephalus.
Long-term HRQoL may decline after surgery.
monitoring: Discuss location-specific and general surgical risks before intervention.
Assess neurological and cognitive function.
Use postoperative MRI follow-up according to tumor grade.

therapies_index.name: gross total resection
approved_indications: Surgical goal when complete removal, including involved dura and bone, is safely feasible.
A goal for spinal meningioma surgery, including in elderly patients.
therapies_index.administration: Complete removal is pursued only when it does not compromise neurological or cognitive function.
monitoring: Determine the extent of resection.
Follow with MRI according to WHO grade.

therapies_index.name: subtotal resection
approved_indications: A planned approach when complete removal would threaten neurological function.
An approach for large skull base meningiomas with high surgical risk, followed in selected cases by treatment of the residual tumor.
therapies_index.administration: Residual tumor may subsequently be observed or treated with postoperative conformal fractionated RT or stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS).
monitoring: Assess the residual meningioma by imaging.

therapies_index.name: Simpson grade I resection
approved_indications: Surgical goal for WHO grade 1 meningioma when safely achievable.
Recommended extent of resection for WHO grade 2 meningioma.

therapies_index.name: preoperative embolization
approved_indications: Not recommended routinely; the surgical team may consider it individually when feeding arteries are inaccessible during surgery, such as in petroclival meningioma.
therapies_index.administration: In the described setting, embolization aims to occlude the meningeal branch of the ascending pharyngeal artery or the tentorial branch of the internal carotid artery.
key_toxicities: Associated with an increased risk of postoperative cardiovascular complications.

therapies_index.name: minimally invasive and endoscopic techniques
approved_indications: Approaches assessed for anterior skull base tumors; superiority over open craniotomy has not been shown.

therapies_index.name: open craniotomy
approved_indications: A valid approach to resect anterior skull base tumors.

therapies_index.name: adaptive hybrid surgery
approved_indications: An emerging approach that deliberately leaves a small residual tumor volume for postoperative SRS.
therapies_index.administration: Intra-operative imaging can support the surgical approach.

therapies_index.name: radiosurgery
approved_indications: A possible alternative to surgery for selected small tumors, locations, or clinical circumstances.
An option for an inoperable or recurrent tumor requiring treatment when its size and proximity to critical structures permit.
An option for small tumors in elderly or critically sick patients.
monitoring: Assess local tumor control.
In skull base meningioma, assess cranial nerve function over time.

therapies_index.name: stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS)
approved_indications: An alternative to surgery in selected patients with small tumors.
A postoperative option for residual meningioma, including intentionally retained skull base tumor.
therapies_index.administration: The guide reports use for intracranial meningiomas with a diameter of 3 cm or less and describes single-dose treatment as an option for spinal meningioma.
key_toxicities: Cranial nerve deterioration was reported after treatment of skull base meningiomas.
monitoring: Assess local control and cranial nerve function.

therapies_index.name: fractionated radiosurgery
approved_indications: An option when a tumor cannot be treated in a single fraction.
An option for WHO grade 1 meningioma when surgery is not possible and treatment is needed.
An approach used for skull base meningiomas, particularly perioptic tumors.
therapies_index.administration: The described multisession approaches commonly use two to five fractions of 4-10 Gy per fraction, for total doses of 18-25 Gy.
monitoring: Assess local control and cranial nerve function.

therapies_index.name: hypofractionated RT
approved_indications: An approach studied for skull base meningiomas.
monitoring: Assess tumor size and local control.

therapies_index.name: Cyber Knife-based hypofractionated radiosurgery
approved_indications: A short-course option evaluated for skull base meningiomas.
therapies_index.administration: The cited multicenter comparison used a median 5 sessions.
monitoring: Assess local control and toxicity.

therapies_index.name: fractionated stereotactic RT
approved_indications: An approach evaluated for skull base meningiomas.
therapies_index.administration: The cited multicenter comparison used a median 33 sessions.
monitoring: Assess local control and toxicity.

therapies_index.name: fractionated radiotherapy (RT)
approved_indications: An option for inoperable or recurrent meningioma requiring treatment.
An option after incomplete resection.
Recommended for recurrent or atypical meningiomas and after Simpson IV-V resection of WHO grade 2 meningioma.
Recommended after feasible radical surgery for WHO grade 3 meningioma.
key_toxicities: Potential long-term effects include neurocognitive impairment, hypopituitarism, and secondary radiation-induced tumors.
monitoring: Assess tumor recurrence and treatment toxicity.

therapies_index.name: fractionated external beam RT
approved_indications: An option when surgery cannot be performed safely or after incomplete resection.
An option when WHO grade 1 meningioma cannot be treated in a single fraction.
key_toxicities: Potential long-term RT effects include neurocognitive impairment, hypopituitarism, and secondary radiation-induced tumors.
monitoring: Assess recurrence and toxicity.

therapies_index.name: postoperative conformal fractionated RT
approved_indications: An option for residual meningioma after planned subtotal resection.
monitoring: Assess the residual tumor.

therapies_index.name: intensity-modulated or 3D conformal RT
approved_indications: Modalities used in the cited NRG Oncology/RTOG 0539 study for intermediate-risk meningioma.
therapies_index.administration: The cited study delivered 54 Gy in 30 fractions.
key_toxicities: The cited intermediate-risk study reported adverse events limited to grade 1 and 2.
monitoring: Assess progression, local failure, and adverse events.

therapies_index.name: intensity modified radiotherapy
approved_indications: Treatment used in a cited NRG Oncology/RTOG 0539 report for high-risk meningioma.
therapies_index.administration: The cited report used 60 Gy/30 fractions.
key_toxicities: In that high-risk cohort, combined acute and late adverse events occurred in about 40% of patients and were limited to CTCAE grades 1-3, except for 1 single necrosis-related death.
monitoring: Assess progression, local control, and adverse events.

therapies_index.name: radionuclide therapy
therapies_index.mechanism: Uses ligands directed at somatostatin receptors expressed by meningiomas.
approved_indications: An experimental approach for meningioma; small studies indicate limited activity and controlled data are lacking.
therapies_index.administration: The guide describes use of ligands such as DOTATOC or DOTATATE without a treatment schedule.

therapies_index.name: DOTATOC
therapies_index.mechanism: A somatostatin receptor-directed ligand described for radionuclide therapy.
approved_indications: Mentioned as a ligand for experimental radionuclide therapy of meningioma.

therapies_index.name: DOTATATE
therapies_index.mechanism: A somatostatin receptor-directed ligand described for radionuclide therapy.
approved_indications: Mentioned as a ligand for experimental radionuclide therapy of meningioma.

therapies_index.name: bevacizumab
therapies_index.mechanism: The guide describes its use as systemic treatment targeting VEGF-dependent pathways.
approved_indications: May be considered only when no further local treatment option exists.
Studied in recurrent or progressive WHO grade 2 and 3 meningiomas; findings from uncontrolled studies require confirmation before routine clinical use can be recommended.

therapies_index.name: vatalanib
therapies_index.mechanism: Described among anti-angiogenic compounds evaluated for meningioma.
approved_indications: Studied in WHO grade 2 and 3 meningiomas recurring or progressing after surgery and RT; uncontrolled results require confirmation before clinical use can be recommended.

therapies_index.name: sunitinib
therapies_index.mechanism: Described among anti-angiogenic compounds evaluated for meningioma.
approved_indications: Studied in WHO grade 2 and 3 meningiomas recurring or progressing after surgery and RT; uncontrolled results require confirmation before clinical use can be recommended.

therapies_index.name: Hydroxyurea
approved_indications: Studied after failure of surgery and RT in WHO grade 1 meningioma without relevant activity; also evaluated in WHO grade 2 and 3 meningiomas without sufficient evidence to recommend routine clinical use.

therapies_index.name: temozolomide
approved_indications: Studied after failure of surgery and RT in WHO grade 1 meningioma without relevant activity or sufficient evidence for routine clinical use.

approved_indications: Studied after failure of surgery and RT in WHO grade 1 meningioma without relevant activity; also evaluated in WHO grade 2 and 3 meningiomas without an established recommendation for routine use.

approved_indications: In a cited randomized phase III trial for WHO grade 1 meningioma, it failed to improve failure-free survival or OS; the guide does not recommend it for routine clinical use.

approved_indications: Evaluated in WHO grade 2 and 3 meningiomas without an established recommendation for routine use.

approved_indications: Evaluated in WHO grade 2 and 3 meningiomas without an established recommendation for routine use.

therapies_index.name: trabectedin

approved_indications: If available, may be considered for patients with AKTE17K-mutant meningiomas.

therapies_index.name: AZD5363

therapies_index.name: dabrafenib

therapies_index.name: mTOR inhibitors
approved_indications: Investigated in experimental models of KLF4K409Q-mutated meningioma; clinical use is not established.

therapies_index.name: immune checkpoint inhibition
approved_indications: An investigational approach being explored for meningioma.

therapies_index.name: AKT inhibitor

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with incidental, asymptomatic, newly diagnosed or slowly growing tumors.
decision_rules: Choose observation initially when an incidental tumor has no symptoms; persistent radiological growth or new symptoms favor intervention.
Assess cognition when deciding whether to intervene, because impairment favors treatment.

recommended_regimens.name: Observation
recommended_regimens.summary: Use surveillance rather than immediate treatment for an asymptomatic, newly diagnosed or slowly growing meningioma.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a prospective study, none of 64 patients developed tumor-related symptoms during 5 years, although 48 tumors (75%) grew by 15% or more in volume; more than 60% showed self-limiting growth.

response_assessment.timepoint: Annually for 5 years; thereafter, intervals may be extended according to age and clinical condition.
response_assessment.interpretation: Evaluate growth and whether continued observation remains appropriate.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: MRI surveillance generally uses gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted sequences; T2-weighted imaging alone may be considered for small meningiomas.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with symptomatic or growing tumors for whom surgery is feasible.
decision_rules: Treat symptomatic or enlarging disease, with surgery as the initial option.
Aim for Simpson Grade I resection when it can be achieved safely; protect neurological and cognitive function rather than pursuing complete removal at any cost.
If complete removal is unsafe, plan a subtotal resection and subsequently observe or irradiate the residual tumor.

recommended_regimens.name: Surgical resection
recommended_regimens.summary: Remove as much tumor as is safely possible, including involved dura and bone when feasible, to relieve symptoms and obtain tissue for definitive diagnosis and molecular analysis.

not_recommended.name: Preoperative embolization
not_recommended.reason: It is not recommended in routine practice and has been associated with greater postoperative cardiovascular risk; a randomized trial found reduced surgery time as its only potential benefit. The surgical team may consider it individually when feeding arteries cannot be accessed surgically.

response_assessment.method: Histology and assessment of extent of resection
response_assessment.interpretation: Use the WHO grade and residual-tumor status to choose observation or further treatment.

response_assessment.timepoint: Annually for 5 years after treatment; thereafter, intervals may be prolonged according to age and clinical condition.
response_assessment.interpretation: Monitor for recurrence or growth of residual disease.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Discuss site-specific surgical risks, seizures, hydrocephalus and possible postoperative cognitive effects. Routine image guidance is advised; intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring may help limit neurological injury. Store tumor tissue for future molecular testing.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients requiring treatment who have a small tumor without mass effect and a relative or absolute contraindication to surgery, or another clinical circumstance favoring a nonsurgical approach.
decision_rules: Consider radiosurgery when surgery cannot be performed and treatment is needed.
If single-fraction treatment is unsuitable, use fractionated radiosurgery or fractionated external beam RT.

recommended_regimens.name: Radiosurgery
recommended_regimens.summary: Use as a nonsurgical treatment option in selected small tumors when surgery is not possible.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The guideline reports local control in the range of 90% after 10 years. For tumors of a diameter of 3 cm or less, local control after SRS was comparable to Simpson Grade I resection. Two retrospective series reported 10-year recurrence-free survival of 93.4% and 95.7%, respectively, with doses above 13 Gy.

alternative_regimens.name: Fractionated radiosurgery
alternative_regimens.summary: Use fractionated stereotactic treatment when a single fraction is unsuitable.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A tumor cannot be treated with one fraction, particularly because of its volume or proximity to critical structures.

alternative_regimens.name: Fractionated external beam RT
alternative_regimens.summary: Use fractionated external beam irradiation when single-fraction radiosurgery is unsuitable.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A tumor cannot be treated with one fraction; the guideline notes that supporting data for WHO grade 1 tumors concern recurrent, “high-risk” disease.

response_assessment.timepoint: Annually for 5 years after treatment; thereafter, intervals may be prolonged according to age and clinical condition.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Without tissue collection, a higher-grade meningioma or another histology cannot be fully excluded. Fractionated radiosurgery for skull base tumors commonly uses two to five fractions of 4-10 Gy per fraction, totaling 18-25 Gy.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with large skull base tumors for whom complete resection carries substantial surgical risk.
decision_rules: Consider deliberately leaving residual tumor to protect neurological function, followed by radiosurgery or fractionated RT for comprehensive treatment.
Select fractionated irradiation when the residual tumor cannot safely receive single-fraction radiosurgery.

recommended_regimens.name: Subtotal surgery and radiosurgery
recommended_regimens.summary: Combine a planned subtotal operation with irradiation of the intentionally retained tumor to reduce progression risk while limiting surgical morbidity.

recommended_regimens.name: Subtotal surgery and fractionated radiotherapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider planned subtotal removal followed by fractionated irradiation of the residual disease.

alternative_regimens.name: Observation
alternative_regimens.summary: Residual disease may instead be monitored when immediate irradiation is not required.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Particularly relevant when no neurological symptoms or signs remain after incomplete resection.

response_assessment.method: Histology and assessment of residual tumor
response_assessment.interpretation: Determine whether to observe or irradiate the remaining disease.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Preservation of cranial nerve and other neurological function is central to choosing planned subtotal removal.

decision_rules: Observe following complete removal rather than routinely adding postoperative treatment.

response_assessment.timepoint: Every 12 months; after 5 years, every 2 years.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with incomplete resection, particularly those without persisting neurological deficits.
decision_rules: Consider surveillance without immediate postoperative RT when neurological symptoms or signs do not persist.
Consider radiosurgery or RT for residual disease when further local treatment is appropriate.

recommended_regimens.name: Observation
recommended_regimens.summary: A watch-and-scan approach may be used after incomplete resection when the patient has no neurological deficits.

alternative_regimens.name: SRS
alternative_regimens.summary: Treat residual tumor with stereotactic irradiation if postoperative local treatment is selected.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Residual disease warrants treatment and tumor size and proximity to critical structures permit radiosurgery.

alternative_regimens.name: Fractionated RT
alternative_regimens.summary: Treat remaining tumor with fractionated irradiation when local treatment is selected.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Residual disease warrants treatment, including when radiosurgery is unsuitable.

response_assessment.timepoint: Every 12 months; after 5 years, every 2 years.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Incomplete removal does not necessarily require immediate postsurgical RT, especially in the absence of persistent neurological findings.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with newly diagnosed disease, including patients whose presumed meningioma grows rapidly during observation.
decision_rules: Treatment is required for WHO grade 2 disease; operate first to obtain diagnostic tissue and relieve mass effect.
Aim for Simpson grade I removal when safely achievable.
Rapid growth of a radiologically presumed meningioma raises concern for a higher grade or, in particular circumstances, metastasis.

recommended_regimens.name: Surgical resection
recommended_regimens.summary: Perform surgery as initial treatment, seeking Simpson grade I resection while maintaining safety.

response_assessment.interpretation: Use the confirmed grade and completeness of removal to determine postoperative management.

response_assessment.timepoint: Every 6 months for 5 years; thereafter, every 12 months.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The follow-up interval reflects the increased recurrence risk. No established pharmacotherapy is identified.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients following Simpson I-III resection, including newly diagnosed tumors after gross total resection.
decision_rules: Consider observation or postoperative RT after complete resection; whether early adjuvant irradiation lowers recurrence risk remains unresolved.
Weigh possible benefit against late RT toxicity.

conditions.name: meningiomas
conditions.description: These tumors can be suspected on imaging, including when discovered incidentally. Tissue obtained surgically permits a definitive diagnosis under the WHO classification.
conditions.epidemiology: Meningiomas account for 37.6% of primary intracranial and central nervous system tumors. In the US, their annual age-adjusted incidence was 8.58 per 100 000 population in 2012-2016. Incidence rises with age, particularly after 65 years, and is higher among originally Africans than among Caucasians across all grades. Ionizing radiation is associated with increased risk. NF2 is the most common associated genetic condition; affected patients are more likely to have multiple tumors or grade 2 and 3 tumors. Longer exposure to exogenous progesterone in females was associated with lower blood levels of progesterone receptor (PR) and NF2 mRNA and was proposed as a possible risk factor.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Tumors may be asymptomatic or cause neurological symptoms, mass effect, or cognitive impairment. Memory, attention, and executive functions are particularly affected. Tumor location, size, and edema have correlated with cognitive decline, although causality has not been established.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Meningiomas are the most frequent intracranial tumors, but the small number of controlled trials has contributed to differences in care between countries and centers. Advances in molecular genetics and trial evidence prompted the European Association of Neuro-Oncology (EANO) to revise its guidance. Neuroimaging, principally MRI, usually provides an initial diagnosis, sometimes incidentally. Observation with serial imaging is suitable for a substantial proportion of patients, particularly those who are asymptomatic or elderly. Definitive WHO classification requires tissue, generally obtained through surgery. Gene-panel sequencing and genomic methylation profiling have an emerging diagnostic role. Complete removal, including affected dura, is often curative. Tumors that require treatment but are inoperable or recurrent may receive radiosurgery when size and nearby critical structures permit, or fractionated RT. Combined surgery and irradiation are used increasingly, although the timing, technique, and dose of RT remain disputed. Somatostatin receptor-targeted radionuclide treatment and all systemic drug approaches remain experimental. Bevacizumab and multikinase inhibitors directed at vascular endothelial growth factor receptor have produced the most encouraging, though modest, drug results; no standard systemic treatment has been established.

document_sections.heading: Key Points
document_sections.content: Observation is the initial choice for incidentally found, asymptomatic, suspected meningiomas. Resection is the initial choice for symptomatic or enlarging tumors. In selected circumstances, radiosurgery or fractionated RT may supplement or replace surgery. Molecular diagnosis is evolving rapidly, and preserving tumor tissue for molecular testing and possible future targeted treatment is strongly recommended.

document_sections.heading: EANO guideline on the diagnosis and management of meningiomas
document_sections.content: EANO published its first meningioma diagnosis and treatment guideline in 2016. Subsequent evidence on clinical decisions, molecular features across WHO grades, controlled studies, and the WHO classification of 2021 led an EANO task force to reassess the literature and update its guidance.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: The EANO task force included neuroradiology, neurosurgery, neuropathology, radiation oncology, and medical neuro-oncology specialists selected across European countries after assessment of their clinical work, research, and guideline experience. The guideline committee defined its subjects and search terms. Authors searched Medline, the Cochrane Library, Embase Ovid, Cancer Net, and Science Citation Index from May 2016 to May 2020; older publications could be included when needed. They considered article types and languages represented within the task force. All authors participated in a consensus review that selected 120 papers. Following European Federation of Neurological Societies guidance, scientific evidence was assigned classes I-IV and recommendations levels A-C. Where evidence was insufficient, the authors gave a “good practice point.”

document_sections.heading: Epidemiology and Risk Factors
document_sections.content: Meningiomas account for the highest incidence share, 37.6%, among primary intracranial and central nervous system tumors. A US registry report issued in 2019 gave an age-adjusted annual incidence of 8.58 per 100 000 population for 2012-2016. Incidence rises with age, particularly after 65 years. Between 2004 and 2010, incidence of WHO grade 2 atypical intracranial meningioma rose from 0.28 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.27-0.29) to 0.30 (95% CI: 0.28-0.32), with an annual percentage change of 3.6% (95% CI: 0.8%-6.5%). Between 2000 and 2010, incidence of WHO grade 3 anaplastic meningioma fell from 0.13 (95% CI: 0.11-0.14) to 0.06 (95% CI: 0.06-0.07), with an annual percentage change of −5.4% (95% CI: −6.8% to −4.0%). Under the WHO classification from 2000, the proportions of intracranial WHO grades 1, 2, and 3 during 2004 to 2010 were 94.6%, 4.2%, and 1.2%, respectively. WHO grades 1 and 2 combined occur 2.3 times more often in females than males; incidence across all grades is higher among people originally from Africa than among Caucasians. Ionizing radiation increases meningioma risk, as observed after medical irradiation and among atomic bomb survivors. Secondary tumors, including meningiomas, after radiosurgery are considered uncommon, at 6.8 cases per 100 000 patient-years. NF2 is the most common associated inherited condition; affected patients more often develop multiple tumors or grade 2 or 3 disease. Studies of hormonal exposure were motivated by higher incidence among women of reproductive age, hormone-receptor expression, an association with breast cancer, and size changes during pregnancy, menstruation, and menopause. One study associated longer exogenous progesterone exposure in females with lower blood PR and NF2 mRNA and proposed a link to greater meningioma risk.

document_sections.heading: Diagnostic Procedures
document_sections.content: The diagnostic discussion addresses imaging, angiographic assessment, histopathology, and molecular pathology. A definitive classification requires examination of tumor tissue, whereas imaging ordinarily establishes a provisional diagnosis.

document_sections.heading: Imaging
document_sections.content: Combined MRI and CT permit a highly probable diagnosis of intracranial meningioma in most cases. Typical findings are isointensity on T1-weighted MRI, hyperintensity on T2-weighted and FLAIR images, marked enhancement, and a peripheral dural tail. Extensive FLAIR edema and heterogeneous enhancement can raise suspicion of WHO grade 2 or 3 histology. Bone-window CT helps assess neighboring hyperostosis and intraosseous spread. Somatostatin receptor 2 expression allows PET delineation after administration of agents such as 68Ga-DOTATATE or 90Y-DOTATOC. Although this is not standardly available, it can help separate tumor from normal tissue and postoperative changes. Figure 1 illustrates 68Ga-DOTATATE PET-CT alongside CT and contrast-enhanced MRI views. Conventional angiography has a diminishing diagnostic role but may help if invasion of a lateral sinus or superior sagittal sinus is suspected and MRI angiography is inconclusive; 3D venous angiography can clarify sinus openness and collateral drainage. Routine preoperative embolization is not recommended because it has been associated with more postoperative cardiovascular complications. A randomized trial identified reduced operating time as its sole potential advantage. The surgical team should decide individually; embolization may help when feeding vessels cannot be reached surgically, including petroclival tumors, with the aim of closing the meningeal branch of the ascending pharyngeal artery or tentorial branch of the internal carotid artery. For observational follow-up, MRI is the reference imaging method. Size is generally assessed on gadolinium-enhanced T1 images; axial T2 images yield comparable measurement information. Surveillance based on gadolinium-enhanced T1 imaging remains a good practice point, although T2-only follow-up can be considered for small lesions. MRI-based machine-learning models may improve diagnosis in selected future settings.

document_sections.heading: Histopathology and Molecular Pathology
document_sections.content: The WHO system describes 15 meningioma subtypes; the document states that 9 are assigned WHO grade 1, 3 WHO grade 2, and 1 WHO grade 3. Grading uses mitotic activity, cerebral invasion, or specified histology. Although studies have questioned its prognostic value, brain invasion remains an independent WHO grade 2 criterion in the WHO classification 2021 after its introduction in 2016. New molecular criteria supplement histology: KLF4/TRAF7 mutations can identify secretory meningioma, while a TERT promoter mutation and/or homozygous CDKN2A/B deletion assigns any meningioma WHO grade 3 regardless of histological anaplasia. Rhabdoid and papillary morphology alone no longer establishes WHO grade 3; these tumors are graded by the criteria used for other variants. Table 1 lists subtype-associated mutations, copy-number changes, and methylation classes. WHO grade predicts outcomes for most patients but has exceptions: some WHO grade 1 tumors relapse unexpectedly early, whereas some completely resected WHO grade 2 tumors remain indolent without postoperative RT. Chromosome 22q deletion and alteration of the other NF2 allele are the most frequent changes across grades. With increasing grade and aggressiveness, NF2-mutant tumors accumulate copy-number changes, commonly beginning with 1p and chromosome 10 deletions; homozygous CDKN2A/B deletion indicates a highly aggressive course and unfavorable outcome independent of histology. In WHO grade 1 NF2 wild-type tumors, reported overall mutation frequencies are AKT1 (up to 20%), SMO (up to 11%), KLF4 (up to 28%), PIK3CA (up to 7%), and TRAF7 (up to 40%). AKT1 and KLF4 often coexist with TRAF7, while TRAF7 alone is unusual. AKT1/TRAF7 and SMO are characteristic of meningothelial tumors, especially at the skull base; KLF4/TRAF7 drives secretory tumors and offers a diagnostic alternative to secretory granules. AKT1 and SMO have been discussed as low-recurrence-risk markers, but independent prognostic studies are inadequate and their association with meningothelial morphology is insufficiently strong for grading. Subtype-enriched or NF2 wild-type-focused studies also prevent reliable conclusions about mutation distribution across all meningiomas. In rare aggressive AKT1- or SMO-mutant disease, these alterations may offer treatment targets, as suggested by a single case. SMARCE1 mutations occur in 97% of clear cell meningiomas. Germline SMARCE1 can predispose to pediatric meningioma, generally spinal, as an alternative to germline NF2; the relative germline and somatic contributions to clear cell disease remain unknown. BAP1 changes occur in some rhabdoid tumors; 2 of 6 BAP1-mutant cases in one report had germline alterations. One papillary-meningioma study found enrichment of PBRM1 mutations. It is unknown whether BAP1 and PBRM1 distinguish the respective tumors with a WHO grade 3-like aggressive course. TERT promoter mutation is an established high-recurrence-risk marker and independent WHO grade 3 criterion; it may arise during progression and be confined to focal aggressive regions, requiring thoughtful tissue sampling. YAP1 fusions can drive pediatric tumors instead of frequently germline-associated SMARCE1, BAP1, or NF2 changes. DNA methylation-based subtyping and proposed classifiers may address subjective histological interpretation and mutation heterogeneity, and may add prognostic information beyond WHO grading and candidate-gene panels. The molecular findings suggest future individualized treatment; tissue sampling and storage for later molecular testing should be routine.

document_sections.heading: Therapeutic Strategies
document_sections.content: Management options include observation, surgery, radiosurgery, fractionated RT, and, when local options are exhausted, investigational systemic treatment. Figure 2 presents decisions based on symptoms or mass effect, clinical condition, WHO grade, and extent of resection. Table 2 pairs drug classes with candidate molecular targets or biomarkers; it does not establish those approaches as effective treatments.

document_sections.heading: Observation
document_sections.content: Wider use of neuroimaging has increased incidental diagnoses. Incidental meningiomas occur on brain MRI in 0.9% to 1.0% of the general population. In a prospective 5-year study, none of 64 patients developed tumor-related symptoms during 5 years, despite volume increases of 15% or more in 48 tumors (75%). More than 60% showed growth that eventually limited itself, supporting serial imaging for asymptomatic tumors until sustained radiological or symptomatic growth. In a separate prospectively followed series of 232 untreated patients observed from 1997 to 2013, Lee et al reported rapid growth in 59 tumors (25.4%). Predictors were size (odds ratio per cm3 1.07, P = .000), absent calcification (odds ratio 3.87, P = .004), peritumoral edema (odds ratio 2.74, P = .025), and T2-weighted hyperintensity or isointensity (odds ratio 3.76, P = .049); those authors proposed a weighted rapid-growth score. Whether every incidental tumor requires prolonged follow-up is debated. Islim et al proposed individualized low-, medium-, and high-risk monitoring based on age, performance status, comorbidities, and MRI features comprising signal intensity, edema, proximity to neurovascular structures, and size. Moreau et al developed diagnostic and prognostic methods and an app. By consensus, suspected meningiomas and WHO grade 1 tumors should receive annual MRI for 5 years, after which the interval may be doubled (good practice point).

document_sections.heading: Surgery
document_sections.content: Surgery is the primary treatment for most symptomatic or enlarging tumors. No randomized trial compares it with other treatments. Institutional series support the prognostic importance of extent of resection, traditionally described with the Simpson classification; trials commonly distinguish gross total removal, meaning no solid residual tumor, from subtotal removal, as adopted by EORTC and RTOG. Surgery should maximize safe removal while minimizing morbidity and preserving neurological function. Removal of all involved dura and bone is the goal when safe, but location, consistency, size, and involvement of critical neurovascular structures constrain what can be removed. Although extent of resection is a modifiable recurrence factor, complete removal must not take precedence over neurological or cognitive preservation. When it cannot be achieved safely, planned subtotal removal is appropriate, followed by surveillance or postoperative conformal fractionated RT or SRS for residual disease. Surgery can relieve symptoms and mass effect and supply diagnostic tissue. Patients should receive discussion of site-specific risks, seizures, and hydrocephalus before surgery. Neurovascular planning, routine image guidance, and integration of datasets such as DOTATATE PET for intraosseous disease can assist surgery. Intraoperative imaging may support adaptive hybrid surgery that intentionally leaves a small residual volume for postoperative SRS. Intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring may reduce neurological injury. Preoperative cognitive impairment merits attention: surgery may improve it, but postoperative impairment is an important risk. Superiority of minimally invasive or endoscopic approaches over open craniotomy for anterior skull-base tumors has not been demonstrated. The same surgical principles apply to the less common spinal tumors. Series generally support attempting gross total removal, including in elderly patients, and report recurrence rates ranging from 1.3% to 14.7%. For spinal disease, the decision between surgery and observation must weigh removal benefits against operative risks.

document_sections.heading: Radiosurgery
document_sections.content: SRS can replace surgery in defined circumstances involving small tumors and elderly or critically ill patients. For intracranial tumors measuring 3 cm or less, reported local control was comparable with Simpson Grade I resection. Two retrospective series linked tumor shrinkage after SRS or hypofractionated RT to durable control at 5 and 10 years; their respective 10-year recurrence-free survival estimates were 93.4% and 95.7% with doses above 13 Gy. Preserving cranial nerves is particularly important at the skull base, motivating combined subtotal surgery and SRS. In a registry analysis of 150 patients receiving both, cranial-nerve function improved in 19% after SRS, while 10% deteriorated 10 years after SRS; deterioration rates were 3.5% after 1 year, 5.5% after 3 years, and 7% after 5 years. Fractionated radiosurgery was developed for larger volumes with the aim of preserving cranial-nerve function, notably for perioptic skull-base lesions. Image-guided frameless delivery permits stereotactically precise multiple sessions; commonly used schedules comprise two to five fractions of 4-10 Gy per fraction and total doses of 18-25 Gy. A pooled comparison across 3 centers found no difference in local control or toxicity between fractionated stereotactic RT (median 33 sessions) and Cyber Knife hypofractionated radiosurgery (median 5 sessions), making the shorter approach a convenient option. Evidence for spinal SRS, whether single-dose or hypofractionated, is limited.

document_sections.heading: Fractionated External Beam RT
document_sections.content: Fractionated external-beam RT remains an important option, including when surgery is unsafe or resection incomplete. Large retrospective reports support earlier EANO guidance with class III evidence and recommendations B and C. A US National Cancer Database series of 7811 patients with WHO grade 2 and 1936 with WHO grade 3 disease treated by surgery and/or RT during 2004 to 2014 reported 5-year OS of 75.9% and 55.4%, respectively (P < .0001). In grade 2 disease, gross total resection and postoperative fractionated RT independently predicted better survival. In the prospective phase II NRG Oncology/RTOG 0539 intermediate-risk cohort, recurrent WHO grade 1 or newly diagnosed completely resected WHO grade 2 tumors received intensity-modulated or 3D conformal RT at 54 Gy in 30 fractions. Among 48 patients evaluable for the primary endpoint, 3-year PFS was 93.8%, estimated 3-year OS was 96%, and local failure was 4.1%. Outcomes did not differ significantly between the specified grade 1 and grade 2 groups, and adverse events were confined to grades 1 and 2. A second report from that trial evaluated 53 high-risk patients with newly diagnosed or recurrent WHO grade 3, recurrent WHO grade 2 after any resection, or newly diagnosed WHO grade 2 after subtotal resection. Following intensity-modified radiotherapy at 60 Gy/30 fractions, 3-year PFS was 58.8%, local control 68.9%, and OS 78.6%, with median follow-up of 4.0 years. Combined acute and late adverse events affected about 40%; events were CTCAE grades 1-3 except for 1 necrosis-related death. In the prospective phase II EORTC 22042-26042 study, 56 patients with newly diagnosed WHO grade 2 disease underwent gross total resection and fractionated RT. Against its primary endpoint of 3-year PFS >70%, estimated 3-year PFS was 88.7%, OS 98%, and local failure 14.3%; grade 3 or higher late toxicity occurred in 14%. Its radiation schedule was 60 Gy in 2.0 Gy fractions, higher than the intermediate-risk NRG/RTOG schedule. The US and European trials suggest possible benefit for intermediate- and high-risk patients with acceptable toxicity, but whether immediate adjuvant RT prevents recurrence after complete WHO grade 2 resection is unresolved. Molecular and DNA-methylation profiling might eventually identify individual recurrence risk and patients most likely to benefit. Avoiding further surgery must be balanced against potential lasting neurocognitive impairment, hypopituitarism, and radiation-induced secondary tumors. The phase III ROAM/EORTC 1308 trial, activated in 2016, compares observation with adjuvant RT after complete resection; its target is 190 patients, with over 60% enrolled at the time described. Its primary measure is MRI-defined recurrence time or PFS, with RT toxicity, quality of life, cognition, time to second-line therapy, OS, and incremental cost per QALY as secondary measures. NRG-BN003 is another enrolling trial. In a database review of 10 458 spinal-meningioma patients from 2004 to 2015, 268 received RT: 131 received surgery plus radiation and 137 radiation alone, including radiosurgery in 61% of the radiation-alone group. Larger size and “borderline” or “malignant” histology were linked to RT use. RT showed no apparent association with OS overall but was associated with reduced mortality in the borderline and “malignant” subset.

document_sections.heading: Pharmacotherapy
document_sections.content: The benefit of systemic drugs remains uncertain because no positive controlled trial supports a firm recommendation. Salvage pharmacotherapy is nevertheless often considered when surgery and RT are no longer feasible. Conventional cytotoxic treatment is generally inactive; in EORTC 1320, trabectedin was not superior to physician's choice for WHO grade 2 or 3 disease after exhaustion of local treatments. Occasional partial responses have been reported, particularly with multikinase inhibitors, and bevacizumab has been reported to slow growth dynamics, suggesting possible activity against VEGF and other kinase-dependent pathways. Interpretation is constrained by small cohorts, mainly retrospective designs, heterogeneous histology and previous therapy, missing comparator groups or dependable historical benchmarks, and nonstandardized response criteria. Recurrent molecular alterations suggest inhibitor targets, but no targeted-therapy trial had been completed. For WHO grade 1 tumors failing resection and RT, retrospective and single-arm phase II studies of Hydroxyurea, temozolomide, irinotecan, interferon-alpha, Sandostatin LAR, pasireotide LAR, imatinib, erlotinib, and gefitinib showed no relevant activity. A randomized phase III trial found no failure-free-survival or OS advantage for Mifepristone. Across available studies, PFS-6 ranged from 0% to 67% and OS from 7 to 13 months. No studied drug had sufficient evidence of clinically relevant activity for routine use; AKT inhibitors, if available, may be considered for AKTE17K-mutant disease. For recurrent or progressive WHO grades 2 and 3 after surgery and RT, studies evaluated hydroxyurea, cyclophosphamide/adriamycin/vincristine chemotherapy, interferonalpha, megestrol acetate, medroxyprogesterone acetate, octreotide, Sandostatin LAR, pasireotide LAR, imatinib, erlotinib, gefitinib, vatalanib, sunitinib, and bevacizumab. PFS-6 ranged from 0% to 64% and median OS from 6 to 33 months. Uncontrolled studies reported the most promising findings for bevacizumab, vatalanib, and sunitinib; controlled prospective confirmation is needed before these agents can be recommended clinically.

document_sections.heading: Cognitive Functioning
document_sections.content: Cognition may be impaired before or after meningioma surgery, chiefly in memory, attention, and executive functioning. Preoperative problems may relate to tumor location or raised intracranial pressure from the lesion or associated edema. Frontal or temporal location, size, and edema volume correlated with decline, but causation was not established. Surgery generally benefited cognition, although postoperative impairment may relate to antiepileptic medication. Several postoperative studies found no clear relationship with tumor side. Marked preoperative edema increases the risk of longer-term postoperative cognitive limitations. Studies found no correlation between RT and cognition. Epilepsy, mood, steroid use, and quality of life were not systematically evaluated as additional influences.

document_sections.heading: Quality of Life
document_sections.content: Before surgery, neurological manifestations and illness-related factors such as antiepileptic medication impair HRQoL. After surgery, patients with meningioma may have better HRQoL than patients with brain cancer, but rapid neurological improvement does not preclude a significant long-term decline. Reported difficulties include cognition, emotional and social functioning, sleep, and fatigue; the proportions able to drive or work decline over time. Lower HRQoL has been associated with larger tumors, higher WHO grade, recurrence, shorter time since diagnosis, age of 50 years or more, greater posttraumatic stress, personality change, confusion, left-hemispheric location, headache, and seizures. Follow-up should assess this long-term burden and consider appropriate interventions.

document_sections.heading: Future Directions
document_sections.content: The document discusses investigational somatostatin receptor-directed radionuclide treatment, laboratory models for evaluating candidate drugs, and therapies guided by molecular alterations. These approaches require further validation and are not presented as established routine treatment.

document_sections.heading: Radioimmunotherapy
document_sections.content: Somatostatin receptor expression has enabled investigational radionuclide treatment with ligands including DOTATOC and DOTATATE. Small studies suggest limited activity, with apparently better local control in lower-grade tumors that express more of the target. Controlled evidence is absent, and most participants had already received multiple interventions, including RT, making major benefit unlikely.

document_sections.heading: Neuropathology
document_sections.content: Assessing candidate treatments, especially for aggressive disease, requires suitable in vitro and in vivo models. Characterized meningioma cell lines differ molecularly and in growth behavior, potentially reflecting the range from ordinary slow-growing to aggressive atypical or anaplastic tumors. Investigators can model somatic mutations through wild-type or mutant overexpression constructs or Crisp-Casmediated editing, then compare drug effects in mutant and wild-type cells. Proposed next steps for in vivo testing include transplantation of engineered cells into nude mice or treatment of genetically engineered mice that develop meningeal tumors. Some established cell lines grow orthotopically in mice. A model containing the secretory-meningioma KLF4K409Q mutation has been used to examine sensitivity to mTOR inhibitors. Patient-material xenografts are difficult because of slow growth and a low successful-engraftment fraction; studies of patient-derived orthotopic xenografts characterized by typical meningioma mutations were unavailable.

document_sections.heading: Pharmacotherapy
document_sections.content: Potential future drug targets include NF2/merlin loss, AKT1, SMO, PIK3CA, VEGF/VEGFR2, BRAF, telomerase activity, and PD-1/ PD-L1. Molecular testing is not yet routine neuropathology, and clinical evidence for acting on these targets is very limited. One patient with AKT1E17K had a response lasting more than 12 months to AZD5363. Another patient with V600E, CDKN2A/2B loss, and APC I13970K showed activity with dabrafenib. Immune checkpoint inhibition is under investigation. Prospective trials with adequate methods are required to validate these possibilities. Table 2 summarizes candidate molecular targets and corresponding drug classes.

document_sections.heading: Special recommendations
document_sections.content: Table 3 summarizes the guideline's key recommendations and their evidence classifications. They include MRI-based radiological diagnosis and follow-up; use of somatostatin receptor II-directed PET when tumor extent or recurrence is uncertain; tissue collection for molecular analysis; observation for appropriate asymptomatic patients; assessment of cognition and HRQoL; surgery as the initial intervention when treatment is needed, aiming for safely feasible Simpson Grade I resection; selected use of radiosurgery or fractionated RT; combined subtotal surgery and irradiation where appropriate; and restricting consideration of bevacizumab or multikinase inhibitors targeting VEGF receptors to situations without another local treatment option. The table assigns GPP to MRI-based radiological diagnosis, molecular tissue collection, HRQoL consideration, and grade-specific MRI follow-up. It assigns 3 C to first-line observation and cognitive assessment, 2 B to radiosurgery or fractionated radiosurgery for WHO grade 1 disease when surgery is impossible and treatment is necessary, 3 C to observation after incomplete WHO grade 1 resection without neurological deficits, and 2 B to fractionated RT for recurrent or atypical meningioma. The document also identifies recommendations revised or newly introduced since 2016.

document_sections.heading: WHO grade 1 meningiomas
document_sections.content: Management should reflect clinical circumstances and major prognostic factors. For an incidental, asymptomatic tumor, initially annual MRI observation is preferred (evidence level III, recommendation level C). Neurological evaluation should pay particular attention to cognition because impairment favors intervention. Symptoms or growth indicate treatment, with surgery first: Simpson grade I removal can often cure, improve neurological or cognitive manifestations, establish a tissue diagnosis, and provide material for molecular testing. Tissue should be stored for possible future targeted therapy (good practice point). Possible immediate and lasting effects of surgery on cognition and HRQoL must also be weighed. For small tumors without mass effect when surgery is relatively or absolutely contraindicated, radiosurgery may be an alternative, although higher grade or another histology cannot be excluded definitively. Reported local control is in the range of 90% after 10 years. Radiosurgery can also treat intentionally retained tumor after subtotal removal of a large, surgically high-risk skull-base lesion. Fractionated radiosurgery or conventional fractionated external-beam RT may be used when single-fraction treatment is unsuitable; evidence for this approach in WHO grade 1 disease comes only from recurrent, “high-risk” tumors. Incompletely resected tumors may not need immediate postoperative RT, especially without remaining neurological signs or symptoms. Effective drug treatment has not been established. For suspected tumors or after treatment, annual MRI is recommended for 5 years; subsequent spacing may be adjusted to age and clinical condition (good practice point). Somatostatin receptor II-directed PET detects tumor tissue with high sensitivity and specificity.

document_sections.heading: WHO grade 2 meningiomas
document_sections.content: Rapid growth of a radiologically presumed meningioma during observation warrants suspicion of higher-grade disease or, in some cases, metastasis. Treatment of confirmed WHO grade 2 disease is mandatory. Surgery is the first choice to establish histology and relieve mass effect, aiming for Simpson grade I resection. Because recurrence risk is increased, MRI follow-up should occur every 6 months for 5 years and annually afterward. Evidence for fractionated RT is increasing, but without completed randomized trials there is only level IV evidence on irradiation after Simpson I-III resection. RT is recommended after Simpson IV-V resection. No pharmacotherapy is established.

document_sections.heading: WHO grade 3 meningiomas
document_sections.content: These tumors grow rapidly, recur early, can metastasize systemically, and have distinctive genetic and epigenetic features. The recommended approach is radical surgery as far as feasible, followed by fractionated RT. No defined role exists for pharmacotherapy. MRI follow-up depends on clinical progression and should take place at least every 3-6 months (GPP).

document_sections.heading: Spinal meningioma
document_sections.content: Surgical removal is the preferred treatment. Simpson grade I or II resection should decompress the spinal cord and remove the tumor; gross total removal should also be attempted in elderly patients. Evidence concerning RT for spinal meningioma is sparse.
